rst31-v2-r2-hyg-q001.stem: Which plan correctly addresses chemical contamination and fish parasites?
options: Ordinary heating always removes chemicals; appearance proves parasite safety
Handwashing alone solves both
Leave both at room temperature
Prevent chemical entry; prevent parasite attachment and apply necessary inactivation
rst31-v2-r2-hyg-q001.explanation: Controls must fit the hazard. Chemical-entry prevention cannot replace parasite prevention and inactivation.
reasons: Ordinary heating does not guarantee chemical removal; appearance does not establish parasite safety
Handwashing alone cannot replace these controls
Room-temperature storage controls neither hazard
It matches different controls to each hazard

rst31-v2-r2-hyg-q002.stem: Which comparison of bacterial and viral prevention is appropriate?
options: Viral entry and spread need no attention
Viral control completes all bacterial control
Only limit multiplication for both
Prevent bacterial attachment, growth and survival; also prevent viral entry and spread
rst31-v2-r2-hyg-q002.explanation: Use the three bacterial principles and combine viral controls with preventing entry and spread.
reasons: Preventing entry and spread is necessary
Controlling one hazard does not replace controlling another
Growth control alone is insufficient
It distinguishes the required combinations

rst31-v2-r2-hyg-q003.stem: Which category includes enterohemorrhagic E. coli, Salmonella and Staphylococcus?
options: Viral
Bacterial
Chemical
Parasitic
rst31-v2-r2-hyg-q003.explanation: All three are bacterial examples, unlike norovirus or Anisakis.
reasons: They are not a group of viruses
All three are correctly classified as bacteria
They are not chemicals such as cleaning agents
They are not a group of parasites

rst31-v2-r2-hyg-q004.objective: Prevent the Salmonella route through raw or undercooked meat.
rst31-v2-r2-hyg-q004.stem: Meat may carry Salmonella. Which decision is appropriate?
options: Avoid raw or insufficiently cooked meat and verify suitable heating
Warm only the surface without checking the center
Fresh meat poses no raw-consumption risk
Only eggs are involved, so meat needs no controls
rst31-v2-r2-hyg-q004.explanation: Salmonella also concerns meat. Freshness or surface appearance cannot rule out hazards from raw or insufficiently cooked meat.
reasons: It prevents the contaminated-meat exposure route
Surface heating does not establish sufficient center heating
Freshness cannot guarantee absence of bacteria
Meat also requires control; this is not limited to eggs

rst31-v2-r2-hyg-q005.objective: Check heating appropriate for norovirus in bivalves.
rst31-v2-r2-hyg-q005.stem: Bivalves may be contaminated with norovirus. What must be checked before serving?
options: Decide safety from shell color
Omit heating checks after handwashing
Verify sufficient heating under the center-temperature and time procedure for this food and hazard
Use a general heating guide without checking applicability
rst31-v2-r2-hyg-q005.explanation: Undercooked contaminated bivalves are an exposure route. Verify applicable heating; handwashing does not replace it.
reasons: Shell color does not verify heating
Handwashing does not remove the need for heating controls
It checks adequate heating for the food and hazard
Do not apply a general guide unconditionally

rst31-v2-r2-hyg-q006.objective: Classify foods by their heating and cooling history.
rst31-v2-r2-hyg-q006.stem: Curry, soup, sauce, dipping sauce and potato salad are heated then cooled. How should they be classified?
options: Skip cooling controls based on the food name
Treat all as unheated
Reheating removes the need for cooling history
Manage both heating and cooling as the relevant process group
rst31-v2-r2-hyg-q006.explanation: These are examples of foods with heating and cooling. Follow actual processes rather than fixing the category by name alone.
reasons: The name does not justify skipping cooling
Do not erase the heating step
Reheating does not replace checking cooling
It controls both actual processes

rst31-v2-r2-hyg-q007.objective: Record daily heating results and abnormalities.
rst31-v2-r2-hyg-q007.stem: Heating work has finished for the day. Which record fits the source example?
options: Record the daily heating result and abnormalities, and follow additional shop requirements
Ignore individual shop records because the source gives an example
Record no abnormalities
Omit the daily result if appearance was normal
rst31-v2-r2-hyg-q007.explanation: The example requires the final daily result and details of problems. Additional shop recording requirements still apply.
reasons: It satisfies both the example and shop requirements
The example does not cancel additional requirements
Abnormalities must also be recorded
Keep the daily result

rst31-v2-r2-hyg-q008.objective: Prepare raw seafood and prevent foreign objects.
rst31-v2-r2-hyg-q008.stem: Which approach correctly combines raw-seafood preparation and foreign-object prevention?
options: Inspect only at delivery, never during preparation
Seawater soaking eliminates all hazards
Wash in suitable fresh water, remove contamination concerns, inspect ingredients and work, and keep order
Tidying removes the need for washing and removal
rst31-v2-r2-hyg-q008.explanation: Use suitable fresh-water washing and removal for raw seafood. Ingredient and in-process checks plus order reduce foreign-object routes.
reasons: Objects can enter during preparation
Seawater alone cannot eliminate every hazard
It combines preparation and continuing prevention
Order does not replace required washing or removal

rst31-v2-r2-hyg-a-group3.title: From food names to process history
rst31-v2-r2-hyg-a-group3.text: If sauce was cooked and cooled yesterday, do not classify it only by how it is served today. Curry, soup, sauce, dipping sauce and potato salad are source examples of foods involving heating and cooling. Write down each actual process and control cooling after heating. The same name can require different controls when preparation differs.
